prog-fond-041.question: A signal occurring during a blanking period is completely ignored by the pacemaker, whereas a signal occurring in the unblanked part of a refractory period can be counted by certain algorithms (e.g. mode switching).
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: during blanking nothing is seen; during the rest of the refractory period the signal is seen and can be used by algorithms.
Incorrect: the distinction is real: this is why AF waves falling in the PVARP (outside the PVAB) count towards mode switching.
prog-fond-041.explication: During blanking, the amplifier is "blind": no signal is seen. During the rest of the refractory period, the signal is sensed but does not reset the timing intervals; it can, however, be used by algorithms. Thus, AF waves falling in the PVARP (outside the PVAB) are taken into account for atrial tachycardia detection and mode switching. This distinction explains why atrial flutter can be undersensed if its waves fall in the blanking period.
prog-fond-041.aRetenir: Blanking = signal invisible; refractory period = signal seen but with no effect on timing.

prog-fond-042.question: DDD: maximum tracking rate 120 bpm, sensed AV delay 180 ms, PVARP 300 ms. Describe the behaviour as the sinus rate accelerates beyond 120 bpm.
prog-fond-042.reponseAttendue: TARP = 480 ms, 2:1 block point = 125 bpm. Between 120 and 125 bpm: pseudo-Wenckebach behaviour (progressive lengthening of the AV delay, then a non-tracked P wave); above 125 bpm: abrupt 2:1 block (ventricular rate halved).
prog-fond-042.explication: The maximum tracking rate interval is 500 ms and the TARP is 180 + 300 = 480 ms. Pseudo-Wenckebach behaviour is possible only if the upper rate interval is longer than the TARP: here the window extends only from 120 to 125 bpm (60,000/480). Beyond that, every other P wave falls in the PVARP: the ventricular rate drops abruptly to around 62 bpm, which may be poorly tolerated on exertion. To widen the Wenckebach window, shorten the PVARP or the AV delay (dynamic AV delay), or raise the upper rate if appropriate.
prog-fond-042.aRetenir: Wenckebach between the maximum tracking rate and 60,000/TARP; beyond that, 2:1 block.

prog-fond-043.question: In a patient with complete AV block paced in DDD mode, the sinus rate slightly exceeds the maximum tracking rate (but remains below the 2:1 block point). What pattern is seen?
options: Abrupt 2:1 block, with the V rate halved
Immediate switch to DDI via mode switching
Progressive AS–VP lengthening, then a non-tracked P
Asynchronous VOO pacing at the upper rate
commentaires: Incorrect: 2:1 block appears only above 60,000/TARP, a point the sinus rate does not reach here.
Incorrect: mode switching responds to a pathological atrial tachycardia, not to sinus tachycardia.
Correct: the V spike is delayed until the end of the MTR interval, then a P wave falls in the PVARP: pseudo-Wenckebach.
Incorrect: the pacemaker continues to sense and track; it never goes asynchronous to limit its rate.
prog-fond-043.explication: The pacemaker cannot pace the ventricle faster than the maximum tracking rate, so it delays ventricular pacing, which progressively lengthens the apparent AV delay. After a few cycles, a P wave falls in the PVARP and is not tracked, reproducing a Wenckebach-like pattern. 2:1 block appears only above 60,000/TARP. A switch to DDI is a matter for mode switching, which is triggered by atrial tachycardia and not by sinus tachycardia.
prog-fond-043.aRetenir: Above the maximum tracking rate: pseudo-Wenckebach, then 2:1 block.

prog-fond-044.question: A patient with a DDD pacemaker (maximum tracking rate 120 bpm) complains of palpitations, with no known atrial tachycardia. Which mechanism explains this tracing?
options: T-wave oversensing on the ventricular channel
Retrograde P sensed outside the PVARP and tracked
Isolated loss of atrial capture, with no other abnormality
Inappropriate rate response at rest
commentaires: Incorrect: T-wave oversensing would inhibit ventricular pacing rather than accelerate it.
Correct: after the PVC, the retrograde P falls outside the PVARP, is followed by a V spike and conducted retrogradely again: this is PMT.
Incorrect: loss of atrial capture can initiate PMT but cannot on its own sustain a paced tachycardia.
Incorrect: rate response accelerates pacing gradually, without abrupt onset after a PVC or retrograde P waves.
prog-fond-044.explication: After a PVC, the tracing shows a regular paced tachycardia in which each QRS is followed by a retrograde P wave: this is pacemaker-mediated tachycardia. PMT requires retrograde ventriculoatrial conduction: the retrograde P falls after the PVARP and is tracked with ventricular pacing, which is again conducted retrogradely. The loop runs at (or just below) the maximum tracking rate. It is terminated with a magnet (asynchronous mode) and prevented by extending the PVARP (particularly after a PVC) or with PMT detection algorithms. Rate response can accelerate pacing but does not create this loop mechanism.
prog-fond-044.aRetenir: PMT = a loop via retrograde VA conduction tracked by the pacemaker; magnet and PVARP.

prog-fond-045.question: Which events can initiate pacemaker-mediated tachycardia in a patient with retrograde VA conduction?
options: Premature ventricular contraction
Loss of atrial capture
Atrial undersensing
Extended PVARP
commentaires: Correct: the PVC is the most common trigger: it dissociates A and V and unmasks retrograde conduction.
Correct: without atrial capture, the atrium remains excitable and can be activated retrogradely by the paced QRS.
Correct: atrial pacing following an unsensed P falls in the refractory period and does not capture: same effect as loss of capture.
Incorrect: extending the PVARP is, on the contrary, the means of prevention: the retrograde P falls in the refractory period.
prog-fond-045.explication: Any event that dissociates atrium from ventricle and leaves the atrium non-refractory can unmask retrograde conduction: a PVC (the most common), loss of atrial capture, atrial undersensing (the subsequent atrial pacing pulse falls in the atrial refractory period and fails to capture), as well as PACs and atrial oversensing. The retrograde P is then sensed outside the PVARP and tracked. Extending the PVARP is, on the contrary, the means of prevention: this is why many pacemakers extend it automatically after a PVC.
prog-fond-045.aRetenir: A PVC, loss of atrial capture or atrial undersensing can trigger PMT.

prog-fond-046.question: What is the purpose of mode switching in DDD mode?
options: To avoid tracking AF or rapid flutter
To raise the lower rate during exercise
To go asynchronous in case of interference
To reduce unnecessary atrial pacing at rest
commentaires: Correct: above an atrial rate threshold, the device switches to DDI(R) or VDI(R) so as not to pace the ventricle rapidly.
Incorrect: that is the role of rate response, not mode switching.
Incorrect: switching to asynchronous pacing during interference is a different function (noise mode).
Incorrect: mode switching is not intended to reduce atrial pacing.
prog-fond-046.explication: Without mode switching, a DDD pacemaker would track AF or flutter by pacing the ventricle up to the maximum tracking rate, irregularly and with poor tolerance. When the device detects an atrial rate above a programmed threshold, it switches to a non-tracking mode (DDI(R) or VDI(R)) and returns to DDD at the end of the episode. Episodes are stored, which also makes mode switching a diagnostic tool for AF. Switching to asynchronous mode during interference is a different function (noise mode).
prog-fond-046.aRetenir: Mode switching = switching to a non-tracking mode during atrial tachycardia.

prog-fond-047.question: A patient with a DDD pacemaker has atrial flutter at 300 bpm with 2:1 conduction. The pacemaker does not mode-switch. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Flutter is never sensed by an atrial lead
The maximum tracking rate is programmed too low
Rate response is switched off on this device
Every other F wave falls in the PVAB and is not counted
commentaires: Incorrect: flutter is usually well sensed; the problem here lies with blanking.
Incorrect: the MTR limits tracking but does not determine detection of the atrial arrhythmia.
Incorrect: rate response plays no part in triggering mode switching.
Correct: with 2:1 conduction, every other F wave coincides with the QRS: the atrial channel counts only about 150 bpm, below the mode-switch threshold.
prog-fond-047.explication: With a flutter cycle length of 200 ms and a QRS every second F wave, every other F wave coincides with the ventricular event and falls in the post-ventricular atrial blanking period. The atrial channel then counts only half the waves, i.e. about 150 bpm, often below the atrial tachycardia detection rate: no mode switching occurs. Some algorithms look specifically for this pattern (temporarily altering timing intervals to unmask hidden waves). Shortening the PVAB, when far-field sensing allows, may also help.
prog-fond-047.aRetenir: 2:1 flutter: every other F wave may be hidden by blanking, preventing mode switching.

prog-fond-048.question: A high number of stored mode-switch episodes is sufficient to diagnose AF and start anticoagulation, without reviewing the EGMs.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: far-field R waves, noise or myopotentials can distort the counters; EGMs must confirm AF before any anticoagulation.
Correct: the stored EGMs must be reviewed, then episode duration and thromboembolic risk taken into account.
prog-fond-048.explication: Mode-switch counters can be distorted by far-field R-wave, noise or myopotential sensing on the atrial channel. Guidelines require review of the stored EGMs to confirm that these are genuine episodes of AF or atrial tachycardia (AHRE/subclinical AF) before any therapeutic decision. The decision to anticoagulate then depends on episode duration and the thromboembolic risk profile. Reviewing the tracings is therefore essential.
prog-fond-048.aRetenir: Mode-switch episodes: always review the EGMs before concluding that AF is present.

prog-fond-049.question: What is a known limitation of an accelerometer-based activity sensor?
options: Weak response to exercise with little trunk movement
Very slow response, over several minutes, at exercise onset
Incompatibility with dual-chamber pacing
Systematic interference with device telemetry
commentaires: Correct: the accelerometer measures movement, which is poorly proportional to metabolic demand: cycling, isometric effort or emotion fool it.
Incorrect: the accelerometer responds quickly at exercise onset; it is minute ventilation that is slower.
Incorrect: accelerometer-based rate response is used in DDDR as well as VVIR.
Incorrect: the activity sensor does not interfere with telemetry.
prog-fond-049.explication: The accelerometer detects body movement and vibration: its response is rapid at the onset of exercise, but poorly proportional to metabolic demand. Isometric exercise or exercise with little trunk movement (cycling) and non-mechanical stress produce little acceleration. Conversely, passive vibration (a vehicle on a cobbled road) may accelerate pacing unnecessarily. The minute ventilation sensor is more physiological but slower; some devices combine the two.
prog-fond-049.aRetenir: Accelerometer: fast, but poorly proportional to metabolic demand.

prog-fond-050.question: A minute ventilation sensor estimates ventilation by measuring transthoracic impedance. Which situation can cause inappropriate acceleration of pacing?
options: Moderate exercise on an exercise bike
Mode switching during AF
A monitor measuring thoracic impedance
A lower rate programmed at 50 bpm
commentaires: Incorrect: exercise physiologically increases ventilation: the acceleration is then appropriate.
Incorrect: mode switching alters atrial tracking, not the transthoracic impedance measurement.
Correct: impedance-based respiratory monitoring (or diathermy, mechanical ventilation) can mimic hyperventilation.
Incorrect: the lower rate has no effect on the minute ventilation sensor.
prog-fond-050.explication: The minute ventilation sensor injects small current pulses and measures the changes in transthoracic impedance caused by respiration. External signals of the same kind (impedance-based respiratory monitoring by some monitors, mechanical ventilation, electrosurgical diathermy) can be interpreted as hyperventilation and drive pacing up to the maximum sensor rate. This is why switching off this sensor is recommended in the perioperative period. Exercise on a bike, by contrast, physiologically increases ventilation.
prog-fond-050.aRetenir: Minute ventilation sensor: switch it off during impedance monitoring or perioperatively.

prog-fond-051.question: Lower rate 60 bpm with rate hysteresis at 50 bpm. What does the pacemaker do?
options: It paces continuously at 50 bpm, day and night
It allows intrinsic rhythm down to 50 bpm, then paces at 60
It paces at 60 bpm as soon as the rhythm drops below 60
It alternates between 50 and 60 bpm depending on activity
commentaires: Incorrect: 50 bpm is the limit to which intrinsic rhythm is tolerated, not the pacing rate.
Correct: after an intrinsic beat, the escape interval is 1,200 ms; when it paces, it does so at the lower rate.
Incorrect: that is the behaviour without hysteresis.
Incorrect: alternation with activity suggests rate response or a rest rate, not hysteresis.
prog-fond-051.explication: Hysteresis lengthens the escape interval after an intrinsic event: the pacemaker tolerates intrinsic rhythm down to 50 bpm. If it has to pace, it does so at the lower rate of 60 bpm until intrinsic rhythm returns (some devices perform periodic searches). The aim is to favour intrinsic rhythm and save battery. The pitfall: in this patient, a cycle of 1,000 to 1,200 ms without pacing is not oversensing.
prog-fond-051.aRetenir: Hysteresis: intrinsic rhythm is allowed to fall lower before pacing at the lower rate.

prog-fond-052.question: Rate response is indicated in a patient with symptomatic chronotropic incompetence.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: symptomatic chronotropic incompetence is the very indication for rate response (class IIa, ESC 2021).
Incorrect: here the sensor replaces the failing sinus node; this is the textbook indication for rate response.
prog-fond-052.explication: Chronotropic incompetence, i.e. the inability to increase heart rate sufficiently on exertion, is the very indication for rate response: the sensor replaces the failing sinus node. The ESC 2021 guidelines propose rate response (class IIa) in patients with chronotropic incompetence who are clearly symptomatic on exertion; it is also recommended in permanent AF (VVIR). In a patient with normal sinus node function and AV block, P-wave tracking in DDD is sufficient to adapt the rate. Settings should be tailored to the patient's activity (walk test, histograms).
prog-fond-052.aRetenir: Symptomatic chronotropic incompetence = turn on rate response.

prog-fond-053.question: Which of the following strategies aim to reduce unnecessary ventricular pacing in a patient with preserved AV conduction?
options: AV delay hysteresis / periodic search for intrinsic conduction
AAI(R)-type operation with conduction monitoring and switch to DDD(R) in case of AV block
Routine shortening of the AV delay to 100 ms
Lowering the maximum tracking rate
commentaires: Correct: periodic AV delay extension allows intrinsic conduction to emerge.
Correct: these modes pace the atrium while monitoring the ventricle, and switch back to DDD in case of AV block.
Incorrect: shortening the AV delay, on the contrary, increases ventricular pacing.
Incorrect: the maximum tracking rate plays no role in minimising V pacing.
prog-fond-053.explication: There are two main families of algorithms: AV delay extension (hysteresis or automatic search for intrinsic conduction), and modes that operate with atrial-only pacing while monitoring the ventricle, switching back to DDD if AV conduction is lost. Shortening the AV delay, on the contrary, increases ventricular pacing. The maximum tracking rate plays no role in this context. These algorithms are recommended in sinus node dysfunction.
prog-fond-053.aRetenir: Minimising V pacing: extend the AV delay or operate in AAI with a switch to DDD.

prog-fond-054.question: In the SAVE PACe trial (sinus node dysfunction), what was the effect of minimising ventricular pacing compared with conventional DDD?
options: No significant difference in AF
Total mortality halved
More syncope due to AV block
About 40% less persistent AF
commentaires: Incorrect: the reduction in persistent AF was significant.
Incorrect: no effect on mortality was demonstrated.
Incorrect: safety was satisfactory, with no excess of AV block-related events.
Correct: persistent AF 7.9% vs 12.7%, i.e. a relative reduction of about 40%.
prog-fond-054.explication: SAVE PACe randomised patients with sinus node dysfunction and preserved AV conduction to conventional DDD(R) or DDD(R) with ventricular pacing minimisation algorithms. Ventricular pacing fell dramatically and persistent AF was reduced (7.9% vs 12.7%, a relative reduction of about 40%). No effect on mortality was demonstrated. Safety was satisfactory, with no excess of AV block-related events.
prog-fond-054.aRetenir: SAVE PACe: minimising V pacing reduces persistent AF by about 40%.
